title: 2-to-1 games with perfect completeness
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: The course is an exposition of OpenAI's proof (2026) of Khot's 2-to-1 games conjecture with perfect completeness, from three theorems of the literature that are stated as named hypotheses and not proved here: for every fixed delta > 0 it is NP-hard to distinguish 2-to-1 games of value 1 from games of value at most delta. The first lesson defines projection games, their value and their repetition, and builds the base game of the reduction (the manuscript calls it the source game): from a formula, a projection game of value 1 if the formula is satisfiable and of value at most sigma otherwise, with answer sets of sizes 7^t and 2^t. It rests on two theorems that are named hypotheses: a PCP theorem with perfect completeness and the parallel repetition theorem for projection games. The second lesson proves the inverse theorem for tables on matrices over the field with two elements: if a partial table often keeps its value under a random step of rank one, one of its values fills a positive fraction of a slice with a bounded number of row combinations and column values, with bounds independent of the number of columns and of the number of values; it rests on the expansion theorem for Grassmann graphs, the named hypothesis (GE). The third lesson defines the new game: the tree, the function spaces H_D (sums of spans of products of functions from the children), arrays and their joint function, the key of a function (the arguments it uses and its partition into fibres), and the constraints that forget one bit; it proves that every constraint has at most two preimages of every label and that a satisfiable formula gives a labeling satisfying all constraints. The fourth lesson proves the exact relations that every labeling satisfies (joint folding: adding products of rows at lower nodes to a row keeps the question and changes the restored values by the same products; the functional of a response on products of displayed rows), shows that changing one bucket of an array is a step of rank one, and defines the law of the tests: independent base questions at the leaves, a random path, recursive samples with products along the path, uniform arrays off the path, and a constraint at a random level of the path. The fifth lesson starts the proof of soundness with the comparisons of laws: the arrays at one node of the path and below it can be replaced by uniform arrays, with a change of at most (1/2) sqrt(L/n) in total variation for every observation that does not use the continuation of the path (n children, L a bound that does not depend on n); the base questions below a sparse random set of children can be replaced by their projections; a child chosen after looking at the functions is rarely one of these; the two comparisons combine at two levels; and every nonzero functional has a bias of at most (7/8)^R on a sample with R products. The sixth lesson assumes a labeling that satisfies the test with probability at least epsilon: two levels i < j are accepted together with probability at least 3 epsilon^2/4; the answers at the upper level form a partial table on matrices that keeps its value along the step of rank one with a fixed probability; the inverse theorem gives a slice and an affine set z_0 + Z of functionals, normalized and of rank at most one on the products of the rows at every node of the level i, such that on the slice the right answer at the lower level has the upper value M z_0 + y more often than a fixed fraction of the time (Proposition 6.1). The seventh lesson turns this inequality into two decoders: the part of the upper matrix whose buckets lie in the kernel of the row map is hidden from both sides, its law is computed on the right side and has small bias; a lemma on characters gives lists of at most 2/tau^2 heavy characters that contain a character of the coset of every prediction that holds on a slice; the left decoder outputs z(xy) for a random z in z_0 + Z, the right decoder a contraction of a random heavy character, and the two bilinear forms agree on the projected space with a probability gamma_j that depends only on epsilon and on the number of rows at the upper level (Proposition 3.1). The eighth lesson proves that at least half of the agreement of the two decoders comes from left forms of rank at most s on the whole lower space, where s depends only on the agreement probability: with the forms of rank at most s removed, two draws of the lower array in the same class modulo the hidden direction give equal left forms with a fixed probability (resampling, posterior bound, sparse projection); the inverse theorem gives one fixed form of large rank on a fraction of a slice; and a fixed form of rank more than s has a Gram matrix of rank at most one on few arrays of a slice (Lemma 4.1). The ninth lesson bounds this agreement from above: a form z(xy) of rank at most s with z(1) = 1 defines at every leaf an odd list of at most s answers, and agreement makes the lists of the two sides satisfy the game on lists of the base game; the marked children of D_i all of whose random functions are zero are clean with a probability that does not depend on their questions, so the base edges at one leaf of each clean child are independent with their law given everything else, each player computes the data of its decoder from public data and its own questions there, and parallel repetition bounds the agreement by exp(-p_0 n_i^(1/3)/64) when the base game has a value below 1/(2 s^2) (Proposition 5.1). For a large number of children this contradicts the lower bound of the eighth lesson. The tenth lesson chooses the parameters so that the assumptions of the lessons hold for all pairs of levels: the numbers of rows from the root downwards, then the number of repetitions of the base game, then the numbers of children from the leaves upwards; this gives the soundness of the game (Theorem 3.1). It then completes the maps to maps that are exactly 2-to-1, replaces the weights by the uniform law on a list of edges, bounds the size of the game, and proves the theorem from the three named hypotheses (Theorem 6.1).
prerequisites: finite probability spaces; Boolean formulas in conjunctive normal form; the notion of a map computable in polynomial time

checks.reading: The manuscript 'Perfect completeness for 2-to-1 games' (OpenAI, 23 Sep 2026; eight sections, 188 KB of TeX) is being read; on 12 Oct 2026 Sections 1 to 3 (introduction, source games and inverse matrix structure, the tree of function spaces) had been read, with a first-pass check recorded in plan/OPENAI_105_SCOPING_20261012.md. Lesson 1 was written against Sections 1 and 2.1. Every step was derived: randomness does not raise the value; the conversion of the PCP instance to a 3-formula with three different variables per clause (bit coding with a default symbol, one clause for each rejected assignment, the chain of new variables for wide clauses in both directions, padding with all sign patterns), with the gap theta/(8B), B = 2^w max(1, w - 2); the value of the clause-variable game (1, or at most 1 - gamma/3); surjectivity of the positions; the base game with t from (1 - gamma_0^2/144)^t <= sigma. The exercises were computed by hand. No discrepancy with the manuscript. Lesson 2 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against Sections 2.2 and 2.3. Every step was derived: the chart of graph subspaces and dim(L_M and L_M') = l - rank(M - M'); the two counts of neighbours ((2^l - 1)(2^m - 1) in the chart, twice as many in the Grassmann graph), hence retention at least eta/4; the interval as a slice (row combinations from a basis of A_0, column values from a basis of the orthogonal space of B_0); the lemma on dummy columns (the image slice, the extension L_0, the number 2^(dim W (dim D - rank d)) of preimages); the averaging over the values of the table; the erasure argument for good row fibres. The whole manuscript had been read once by then (plan/OPENAI_105_SCOPING_20261012.md). In the lesson the number of row combinations is called k, because a is also the vector of the step. The exercises were computed by hand. No discrepancy with the manuscript. Lesson 3 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against Sections 3.1 to 3.3 (formal slots and pointwise spaces; joint evaluations and canonical questions; one-bit constraints and perfect completeness). Every step was derived: the properties of the spaces; uniqueness of the position of a reducible clause slot by surjectivity on pairs; the reduced domain and the dependence of the key on the relation of equal values only; the equality of the keys of f and of f composed with the projection; the constraint maps (onto, at most two preimages); completeness by the point given by a satisfying assignment. The lesson writes Theta_{D,a} for the quotient map (the manuscript writes Q_{D,a}) and 'key', 'label', 'restored value' for the manuscript's canonical key, legal label and restored output. The exercises were computed by hand (the dimension 13 in Exercise 6.1; the example of Exercise 6.2 is the manuscript's). No discrepancy with the manuscript. Lesson 4 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against Sections 3.4 and 3.5 (joint folding; joint evaluation of product generators; the distribution of tests). Every step was derived: the triangular shift is an involution of the space of joint values, hence the key is unchanged and the restored values are shifted; the functional b_y is the evaluation at a point that realizes the response; uniform buckets give a uniform array, and resampling the bucket of a gives the step M + a h with h uniform and independent; the sampler and the test law as in the manuscript (p uniform in 1..d, a_p uniform nonzero). The exercises were computed by hand. No discrepancy with the manuscript. Lesson 5 was written on 12 Oct 2026 against Section 4 (stopped calls; one hidden child; sparse projection and its posterior; bias), read a second time line by line. Every step was derived. Differences of presentation: the chi-square distance of a law with density at most L from the uniform law is bounded by L - 1 (the manuscript uses L^2), so the bounds read (1/2) sqrt(L/n) and (1/2) sqrt((1 + beta^2 L)^n - 1), which are at most the manuscript's; the constant R_min is given as 6; the comparison at two levels is a separate proposition with the count of the calls; the description of the array at the cut by rows is derived from the description by buckets. open_obligations: With the tenth lesson the theorem is proved in the course from the three named hypotheses (PCP), (PR) and (GE); these three are not proved in the programme. The computation of the game in polynomial time is proved by counting the objects and bounding their sizes (Proposition 5.2 of the tenth lesson); the course gives no bound for the constants or for the degree of the polynomial. The lessons were written and checked by one model in one session; they have not been checked by a second reader.

Named hypothesis (PCP) of the first lesson: a PCP theorem with perfect completeness in the form of a gap for constraint systems of bounded arity over a fixed alphabet (Dinur 2007, as cited in the manuscript). Not proved in the course; the programme has no course on probabilistically checkable proofs.
Named hypothesis (PR) of the first lesson: parallel repetition for projection games with the bound (1 - g^2/16)^k (Dinur and Steurer 2014, as cited in the manuscript). Not proved in the course.

Named hypothesis (GE) of the second lesson: a set of vertices of a Grassmann graph over the field with two elements with retention at least zeta is dense in an interval of bounded co-order (Khot, Minzer and Safra 2018, as cited in the manuscript). Not proved in the course; it is the deepest of the three external theorems.
Relayed and not checked: the statements about the history of the conjecture and of the theorems (attributed to the manuscript in the lesson).
